title: Lesson 73: Enterprise Integration Patterns: Routers, Translators, Aggregators, and EIP
description: The shared vocabulary of enterprise integration: the Enterprise Integration Patterns (EIP) catalog, the Message Router that decides where a message goes without changing it, the Message Translator that adapts one format or contract to another, and the Aggregator that combines related messages into one result.

questions.question: A Message Router receives one message and must deliver it to one of several channels. What discipline keeps it a router rather than a router and translator combined?
options: It decides the destination only and forwards the payload unchanged.
It rewrites the payload into the target format before forwarding it.
It merges several related messages into one combined payload first.
It holds the message until every downstream channel confirms receipt.
questions.explanation: A router answers only where a message goes; reshaping the payload belongs to a separate translator, which keeps routing rules simple and testable.

questions.question: Two systems integrate today and four more will join next year, each needing its own mapping. Why does a canonical data model reduce the maintenance burden?
options: It forces every system onto one binary wire format, so no mapping is needed again.
It only helps when exactly two systems integrate, so it suits small point-to-point links.
It turns many pairwise mappings into one per system, so the count grows additively.
It removes the need for translators by making every system share a single database.
questions.explanation: Mapping every source to every target grows multiplicatively, while mapping each system to one shared contract grows additively and stays maintainable as systems join.

questions.question: A quoting flow fans a request out to several providers and needs a usable rate quickly, where waiting for every reply would be too slow. Which aggregator design fits?
options: Send every provider reply to its own queue without combining them.
Stop at the first acceptable reply, matched to the request by a correlation key.
Wait for every provider reply before publishing, no matter how long it takes.
Translate each reply into a shared format and publish each reply to its own channel.
questions.explanation: An aggregator needs a correlation key and an explicit completeness condition; stopping at the first acceptable reply trades completeness for latency, which matches a quote.
